questions.keyConcept: Morphine, fentanyl, methadone are strong pure mu opioid agonists - maximum analgesia with respiratory depression risk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the partial agonists opioids?
questions.explanation: Partial agonist opioids include buprenorphine (partial mu agonist) and pentazocine (partial kappa agonist, mixed agonist-antagonist).选项A正确. Buprenorphine is used for opioid dependence (Suboxone) and analgesia. Its ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes it safer. The answer is A. Pentazocine can precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients.
questions.keyConcept: Buprenorphine is a partial mu agonist with ceiling effect on respiratory depression - used in opioid dependence treatment.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drugs are classified as opioid antidiarrheals?
questions.explanation: Opioid antidiarrheals include: loperamide (Imodium), diphenoxylate (with atropine as Lomotil), and opium tincture. These act on mu receptors in the myenteric plexus, decreasing motility and secretion.选项C正确. The answer is C. Loperamide does not cross BBB significantly, avoiding CNS effects.
questions.keyConcept: Loperamide and diphenoxylate are opioid antidiarrheals - mu receptor agonists in the gut decreasing motility.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the cause of iatrogenic Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic Parkinson's disease is caused by drugs that block dopamine receptors: antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, risperidone), antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), and some calcium channel blockers.选项A正确. The answer is A. Drug-induced parkinsonism is reversible upon drug discontinuation but may take weeks to months.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine-blocking drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) cause iatrogenic parkinsonism - reversible upon discontinuation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the aim of drug therapy in Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: The aim of drug therapy in Parkinson's disease is to restore dopamine deficiency and reduce excess cholinergic activity. This involves: dopamine replacement (L-dopa, dopamine agonists), COMT inhibitors (entacapone), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline), and anticholinergics for tremor.选项A正确. The answer is A. Treatment aims to improve motor symptoms and quality of life.
questions.keyConcept: PD drug therapy aims to restore dopaminergic activity and reduce cholinergic excess - improving motor function.
options: To restore balance between dopamine and acetylcholine activity in the basal ganglia
To increase dopamine activity in the basal ganglia
To decrease acetylcholine activity in the basal ganglia

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the first choice agents in early Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: First choice agents in early Parkinson's disease: levodopa/carbidopa combinations (most effective for motor symptoms) and dopamine agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole) as alternatives. MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline) may be used early.选项D正确. The answer is D. Treatment choice depends on age, symptom severity, and cognitive status.
questions.keyConcept: Levodopa/carbidopa and dopamine agonists are first-line for early PD - L-dopa is most effective, agonists delay motor complications.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the classifications of local anesthetics?
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics classified by: 1) Chemical structure - esters (procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine) and amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine); 2) Duration of action - short, intermediate, long-acting.选项C正确. The answer is C. Esters are metabolized by plasma cholinesterase; amides are metabolized in liver.
questions.keyConcept: Local anesthetics are classified as esters vs amides (metabolism) and by duration of action (short/intermediate/long).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Why are vasoconstrictors added to local anesthetics?
questions.explanation: Vasoconstrictors (epinephrine, norepinephrine, felypressin) are added to local anesthetics to: constrict blood vessels, reduce bleeding, decrease systemic absorption, prolong anesthetic duration, and reduce peak plasma levels.选项C正确. The answer is C. Contraindicated in patients with cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, and those on non-selective beta-blockers.
questions.keyConcept: Vasoconstrictors prolong local anesthetic duration and reduce toxicity by decreasing systemic absorption and bleeding.
options: To prolong the duration of action
To reduce systemic adverse effects and bleeding tendency

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: How do general anesthetics inhibit neuronal activity?
questions.explanation: General anesthetics inhibit neuronal activity by enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission (GABA-A receptor activation - barbiturates, benzodiazepines, propofol, isoflurane) or inhibiting excitatory neurotransmission (NMDA receptor blockade - ketamine, nitrous oxide).选项C正确. The answer is C. Some agents do both. The net effect is decreased neuronal excitability and consciousness.
questions.keyConcept: General anesthetics enhance GABA (inhibitory) or block NMDA (excitatory) to inhibit neuronal activity.
options: They facilitate inhibitory effects of GABA at GABA receptors
Inhibit excitatory effects of glutamate at NMDA receptors

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the classic antiepileptic drugs?
questions.explanation: Classic antiepileptic drugs include: phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproic acid, ethosuximide, phenobarbital, and benzodiazepines. These are first-generation drugs with well-established efficacy.选项D正确. The answer is D. They have more drug interactions and side effects compared to newer agents.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, ethosuximide are classic antiepileptics - more side effects and interactions than newer drugs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the newer antiepileptic drugs?
questions.explanation: Newer antiepileptic drugs include: lamotrigine, levetiracetam, topiramate, gabapentin, pregabalin, vigabatrin, tiagabine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide, and zonimide. These have improved side effect profiles.选项D正确. The answer is D. They are often used as adjuncts or alternatives to classic drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Lamotrigine, levetiracetam, topiramate are newer antiepileptics - better tolerated with fewer drug interactions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of antidepressants?
questions.explanation: Antidepressants work mainly by increasing synaptic monoamine levels (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine). SSRIs inhibit serotonin reuptake; SNRIs inhibit both; TCAs inhibit norepinephrine and serotonin; MAOIs inhibit monoamine oxidase.选项C正确. The answer is C. The monoamine hypothesis suggests depression involves decreased serotonin/norepinephrine.
questions.keyConcept: Antidepressants increase synaptic monoamines (serotonin, norepinephrine) via reuptake inhibition or enzyme blockade.
options: Increase brain biogenic amines (norepinephrine and serotonin)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which class of antidepressants is reserved for atypical depression associated with anxiety and phobia?
questions.explanation: MAO inhibitors (MAOIs) like phenelzine, tranylcypromine are reserved for atypical depression associated with hypersomnia, hyperphagia, and mood reactivity.选项A正确. The answer is A. They require dietary restrictions (tyramine avoidance) due to hypertensive crisis risk.
questions.keyConcept: MAOIs are reserved for atypical depression with hypersomnia and hyperphagia - require tyramine dietary restrictions.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which class of antidepressants is the first choice for initial therapy?
questions.explanation: SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram) are first-choice for initial therapy due to: efficacy, once-daily dosing, safety in overdose, and favorable side effect profile.选项B正确. The answer is B. They are better tolerated than TCAs and MAOIs.
questions.keyConcept: SSRIs are first-line antidepressants - safe, effective, once-daily, and favorable side effect profile.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which class of antidepressants is reserved for resistant cases?
questions.explanation: MAOI antidepressants are reserved for resistant cases that fail other antidepressants. They require careful monitoring and dietary restrictions.选项C正确. The answer is C. They are used when SSRIs, SNRIs, and TCAs have failed due to their complexity and risk.
questions.keyConcept: MAOIs are reserved for treatment-resistant depression - require tyramine diet and careful monitoring.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the aim of management for Alzheimer disease?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's management aims to: slow cognitive decline, manage behavioral symptoms, improve quality of life, and support caregivers. Options include cholinesterase inhibitors, memantine, and behavioral interventions.选项C正确. The answer is C. There is no cure - treatment is symptomatic.
questions.keyConcept: Alzheimer's treatment aims to slow progression and manage symptoms - cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are mainstays.
options: Increase cholinergic activity in the brain
Reduce excitotoxicity action of overstimulation of NMDA receptors

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the cholinesterase enzyme inhibitors used in the treatment of Alzheimer disease?
questions.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors for Alzheimer's: donepezil (Aricept), rivastigmine (Exelon), galantamine (Razadyne). These increase acetylcholine in the brain.选项D正确. The answer is D. They provide modest symptomatic benefit.
questions.keyConcept: Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine are cholinesterase inhibitors - modestly effective in Alzheimer's.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the management approach for Multiple Sclerosis?
questions.explanation: MS management: disease-modifying therapies (interferon-beta, glatiramer, natalizumab, fingolimod) for relapsing forms; symptom management; rehabilitation.选项D正确. The answer is D. No cure - treatment aims to reduce relapses and disability.
questions.keyConcept: MS management uses disease-modifying therapies to reduce relapse rate and slow disability progression.
options: Treatment of acute episodes (exacerbations) with corticosteroids

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the first-line therapy drugs used in the treatment of MS?
questions.explanation: First-line MS disease-modifying drugs: interferon-beta preparations (Avonex, Betaseron, Rebif), glatiramer acetate (Copaxone). These reduce relapse rate by ~30%.选项A正确. The answer is A. They are injectables with modest efficacy.
questions.keyConcept: Interferon-beta and glatiramer are first-line MS disease-modifying therapies - reduce relapse rate ~30%.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of typical antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, chlorpromazine) work by blocking D2 dopamine receptors, reducing dopaminergic transmission in mesolimbic pathway (treats positive symptoms).选项A正确. The answer is A. Also blocks D2 in nigrostriatal pathway (causes EPS) and tuberoinfundibular pathway (hyperprolactinemia).
questions.keyConcept: Typical antipsychotics block D2 receptors - therapeutic for psychosis but cause EPS and hyperprolactinemia.
options: Blocking D2 receptors in the mesolimbic system improves positive symptoms

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What receptors do atypical antipsychotics block in addition to D2 receptors?
questions.explanation: Atypical antipsychotics (clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone) block D2 plus serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. This 5-HT2A blockade allows more dopamine in nigrostriatal pathway, reducing EPS.选项A正确. The answer is A. This dual blockade gives atypicals their improved side effect profile.
questions.keyConcept: Atypical antipsychotics block both D2 and 5-HT2A receptors - greater dopamine in motor pathways reduces EPS.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the typical antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Typical antipsychotics include: haloperidol, chlorpromazine, thioridazine, fluphenazine, perphenazine, and flupentixol.选项D正确. The answer is D. They have high D2 affinity and significant EPS risk.
questions.keyConcept: Haloperidol, chlorpromazine, thioridazine are typical antipsychotics - high EPS risk from D2 blockade.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the atypical antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Atypical antipsychotics include: clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone, quetiapine, ziprasidone, aripiprazole, paliperidone.选项D正确. The answer is D. They have lower EPS risk but metabolic side effects.
questions.keyConcept: Clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone are atypicals - lower EPS but weight gain, metabolic syndrome risk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What are the risks of chronic abuse of opioids?
questions.explanation: Chronic opioid abuse risks: respiratory depression, dependence/addiction, constipation, hormonal dysfunction (hypogonadism), hyperalgesia, and infections (HIV, hepatitis from IV use).选项D正确. The answer is D. Opioid tolerance develops, requiring higher doses.
questions.keyConcept: Chronic opioid abuse causes respiratory depression, dependence, constipation, hormonal dysfunction, and infection risk.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: How is opioid abuse managed?
questions.explanation: Opioid abuse management: detoxification (methadone, buprenorphine maintenance), behavioral therapy, naltrexone (opioid antagonist) to prevent relapse, and support groups.选项D正确. The answer is D. Methadone maintenance is gold standard for opioid dependence.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid dependence: methadone/buprenorphine maintenance, naltrexone, behavioral therapy - comprehensive approach.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Extradural hemorrhage is caused by rupture of:
questions.explanation: Extradural hemorrhage caused by rupture of middle meningeal artery (usually from temporal bone fracture).选项C正确. The answer is C. This is a surgical emergency - lucid interval then rapid deterioration.
questions.keyConcept: Extradural hematoma: middle meningeal artery rupture - 'talk and die' syndrome, biconvex shape on CT.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding Evoked brain potentials:
questions.explanation: Evoked potentials represent summation of EPSPs and IPSPs in brain neurons in response to stimuli. They are used for brain mapping, recorded in conscious individuals, and consist of primary (localized) followed by secondary (diffuse) waves. They are NOT due to RAS activity.
questions.keyConcept: Evoked potentials: cortical response to sensory input; EPSP/IPSP summation; primary (specific) then secondary (diffuse).
options: It is used for mapping of the brain.
It is recorded in a conscious person.
It consists of a primary diffuse wave followed by a secondary localized wave.
It is due to activity of RAS.
It represents summation of excitatory and inhibitory potentials in brain neurons

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What does pontine hemorrhage cause?
questions.explanation: Pontine hemorrhage causes pinpoint pupils (due to sympathetic pathway damage), hyperpyrexia (due to hypothalamic dysfunction), and quadriplegia (due to corticospinal tract damage). The pons contains the descending sympathetic pathway and reticular formation.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine hemorrhage: pinpoint pupils, hyperpyrexia, quadriplegia. Disrupts sympathetic pathways and corticospinal tracts.
questions.modelAnswer: Pinpoint pupil (due to disruption of descending sympathetic pathways), hyperpyrexia (damage to hypothalamic temperature-regulating centers), and quadriplegia (bilateral corticospinal tract damage). Also may cause respiratory arrest and loss of consciousness.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What tumor is characterized by excessive production of catecholamines? And what is the treatment of it?
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla; treatment includes alpha-methyl tyrosine (blocks tyrosine hydroxylase) and surgical removal, plus alpha/beta blockers for symptomatic control.
questions.keyConcept: Pheochromocytoma diagnosis and treatment
questions.modelAnswer:
Pheochromocytoma
α-methyl tyrosine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the inhibitor of dopa-decarboxylase used in the treatment of Parkinson Disease?
questions.explanation: Carbidopa is a peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor used in Parkinson's treatment; it prevents peripheral L-DOPA conversion to dopamine, increasing brain delivery and reducing peripheral side effects like nausea.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibition
questions.modelAnswer: Carbidopa

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What enzyme is inhibited by a-methyl tyrosine in the treatment of pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation: Alpha-methyl tyrosine inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, blocking conversion of tyrosine to DOPA and reducing catecholamine production in pheochromocytoma.
questions.keyConcept: Alpha-methyl tyrosine mechanism
questions.modelAnswer: Tyrosine hydroxylase

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Is histamine a vasodilator? If true, what else? And if false, why?
questions.explanation: True, histamine is a vasodilator; another vasodilator neurotransmitter is nitric oxide, which acts via cGMP pathway on vascular smooth muscle.
questions.keyConcept: Histamine and NO vasodilation
questions.modelAnswer:
True
Nitric oxide

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is Myasthenia gravis?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder with antibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing fatigable muscle weakness that worsens with activity.
questions.keyConcept: Myasthenia gravis autoantibody mechanism
questions.modelAnswer: A chronic autoimmune neuromuscular disease causing weakness in the skeletal muscles

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: What is the function of neomycin in the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.explanation: Neomycin treats hepatic encephalopathy by killing intestinal bacteria that produce ammonia from protein catabolism, reducing the ammonia load reaching the liver through portal circulation.
questions.keyConcept: Neomycin ammonia reduction mechanism
questions.modelAnswer: Kills intestinal bacteria

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: To increase the synthesis of catecholamines in the brain, a patient with Parkinsonism may be given
questions.explanation: L-dopa (levodopa) is the direct precursor of dopamine and is administered to increase catecholamine synthesis in Parkinson's disease, where dopaminergic neurons have degenerated. L-dopa crosses the blood-brain barrier unlike dopamine itself, then is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase.
questions.keyConcept: L-dopa as dopamine precursor in Parkinson's disease treatment

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning anesthetics is correct ?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic that blocks NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) glutamate receptors, producing anesthesia with catatonia and analgesia. Thiopental is short-acting due to redistribution, not metabolism; propofol lacks analgesic effect; halothane increases ICP.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine as NMDA receptor antagonist producing dissociative anesthesia
options: Thiopental is ultra short acting due to rapid metabolism.
Propofol possesses a strong analgesic effect.
Halothane is the least likely inhalation agent to increase intracranial tension.
Dissociative anesthesia is induced by midazolam.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following concerning antiparkinsonian drugs is/are CORRECT?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is given subcutaneously in Parkinson's disease emergencies (e.g., akinetic crisis), and amantadine can cause insomnia. Carbidopa does not reduce L-dopa-induced dyskinesia (dopamine agonists do). Benztropine is an anticholinergic for tremor, not fluctuations. Answer E (A and D) is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine SC in emergency; amantadine-induced insomnia in Parkinson's treatment
options: Apomorphine is given subcutaneously in emergency.
L-dopa- induced dyskinesia is reduced by carbidopa.
Benztropine reduces fluctuations in response to L-dopa.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding NSAIDs is FALSE?
questions.explanation: Aspirin is contraindicated in children with viral infections due to Reye's syndrome risk; paracetamol or ibuprofen are preferred. All other statements about NSAIDs (nephrotoxicity, no respiratory depression, no dependence, GI irritation) are true.
questions.keyConcept: Aspirin contraindication in children (Reye's syndrome risk) making the statement FALSE
options: Nephrotoxicity may occur on chronic use of high doses
Respiratory depression seen with opioid analgesics does not occur with therapeutic doses of NSAIDs
Their use does not result in drug dependence seen with opioid analgesics
Aspirin is a good choice for use as analgesic antipyretic for children
They may cause-gastric mucosal irritation and bleeding

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following analgesic agents poses a risk in a 60-year-old patient with a history of transient ischemic attacks
questions.explanation: Celecoxib (a COX-2 inhibitor) increases cardiovascular risk (thrombotic events, stroke) in patients with prior TIA or stroke history. Paracetamol and aspirin are safer options in such patients, with aspirin having protective antiplatelet effects.
questions.keyConcept: COX-2 inhibitors contraindicated in patients with prior TIA/stroke history

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is FALSE concerning selective COX 2 inhibitors ? :
questions.explanation: COX-2 inhibitors were withdrawn (rofecoxib) or carry warnings due to increased cardiovascular risk (heart attack, stroke). They do have low GI ulceration risk and nephrotoxicity concerns. Celecoxib is contraindicated in sulfonamide allergy.
questions.keyConcept: COX-2 inhibitors carry significant cardiovascular risk (heart attack, stroke) - FALSE statement
options: Are associated with low risk of gastric ulceration
Have a low risk of cardiotoxicity and stroke
Nephrotoxicity is a serious adverse effect
Celecoxib should not be given to patients with sulfonamide allergy

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: To increase the synthesis of catecholamines in the brain, a patient with Parkinsonism may be given:
questions.explanation: L-dopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to dopamine by DOPA decarboxylase, increasing catecholamine levels in Parkinson's patients with dopaminergic neuron loss. Alpha-methyldopa is an antihypertensive.
questions.keyConcept: L-dopa administered to increase brain catecholamine synthesis in Parkinson's disease

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Management of phenylketonuria necessitates.
questions.explanation: PKU management requires neonatal screening for early detection, low phenylalanine diet (milk substitutes containing tyrosine), and treatment initiation before one month of age to prevent irreversible brain damage.
questions.keyConcept: PKU management: neonatal screening, low Phe diet, early treatment before 1 month
options: Early detection by routine neonatal screening.
Starting treatment before the age of 1 month.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Pilocytic astrocytoma is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a benign, slow-growing tumor (WHO grade I) with good prognosis, often cystic and occurring in children/young adults in the cerebellum. It is not malignant.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma is benign (WHO grade I) with good prognosis - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Pilocytic astrocytoma shows the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytomas show activation of the MAPK pathway and BRAF alterations (especially BRAF-KIAA1549 fusion). NF1 inactivation is seen in optic pathway gliomas. IDH1/IDH2 mutations are seen in adult diffuse astrocytomas, not pilocytic.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma: BRAF activation, MAPK pathway (NOT IDH1/IDH2 mutations)
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man develops new onset of seizures & headaches. A CT scan reveals a 6 cm left-sided intracerebral mass. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glioblastoma multiforme (WHO grade IV) is the most common and aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, presenting with seizures and headache. It is a diffusely infiltrating astrocytic tumor with necrosis and angiogenesis.
questions.keyConcept: Glioblastoma multiforme: most common aggressive adult brain tumor, seizures, headache

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Astrocytoma is:
questions.explanation: Astrocytomas are tumors derived from astrocytes, classified as grade I (pilocytic, benign) to grade IV (glioblastoma, malignant). They are the most common primary brain tumors, typically in adults.
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytoma: glial tumor from astrocytes, grades I-IV

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Meningioma shows:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas are characterized by psammoma bodies (laminated calcified concretions), whorled patterns of spindle cells, and meningothelial cells. Rosenthal fibers are seen in pilocytic astrocytomas; vascular proliferation in glioblastomas.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma characteristic: psammoma bodies, whorled pattern

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The following is not a feature of meningioma:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas typically have a whorled cut surface (not whorly). The other statements about meningioma (adults, benign, psammoma bodies) are true. The question asks for what's NOT a feature.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma has whorled pattern, not whorly surface - minor terminology

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: The following is not a type of glioma:
questions.explanation: Ganglioneuroma is a benign tumor of mature neurons (not a glioma). Astrocytomas, ependymomas, and glioblastomas are all gliomas (tumors of glial cells).
questions.keyConcept: Ganglioneuroma is NOT a glioma (it's a neuronal tumor) - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Oligodendroglioma is not a:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas are low-grade (grade II) tumors, not high-grade. They are glial tumors, cerebral tumors, and well-circumscribed. High-grade would be anaplastic oligodendroglioma (grade III).
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma is a low-grade tumor, NOT high-grade - EXCEPTION

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Astrocytoma is a:
questions.explanation: Astrocytomas are glial tumors derived from astrocytes, the most common primary brain tumors. They range from grade I (pilocytic, benign) to grade IV (glioblastoma, highly malignant).
questions.keyConcept: Astrocytoma is a glial tumor (from astrocytes)

questions.subject: Histology
questions.text: Oligodendrogliomas are not characterized by:
questions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas do NOT typically show activation of the MAPK pathway. They characteristically have IDH1/IDH2 mutations and 1p/19q codeletion. MAPK activation is seen in pilocytic astrocytomas (BRAF fusion).
questions.keyConcept: Oligodendroglioma: IDH mutation, 1p/19q codeletion (NOT MAPK activation) - EXCEPTION
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Rabies is transmitted to CNS via:
questions.explanation: Rabies virus travels from the bite site via retrograde axonal transport through peripheral nerves to the CNS. This is why post-exposure prophylaxis must be administered promptly before the virus reaches the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Rabies spreads to CNS via retrograde axonal transport through peripheral nerves

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Muscle paralysis in case of poliomyelitis is due to:
questions.explanation: Poliovirus selectively destroys anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) in the spinal cord, causing flaccid paralysis. The muscle paralysis is NOT due to direct viral damage to muscle or toxin production.
questions.keyConcept: Polio paralysis from destruction of anterior horn motor neurons in spinal cord
options: Destruction of the muscle fibers by the toxins of the organisms.
Inflammation of the nerves supplying the affected muscles.
Degeneration of their anterior horn cells in the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Poliomyelitis is a:
questions.explanation: Poliomyelitis is caused by poliovirus, an enterovirus (RNA virus). It is transmitted fecal- orally and causes anterior horn cell destruction leading to flaccid paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: Poliomyelitis is a viral infection (poliovirus, enterovirus)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The cause of death in rabies is:
questions.explanation: Death in rabies is due to respiratory muscle paralysis (bulbar palsy affecting respiratory muscles), not heart failure or direct respiratory center failure. The virus destroys motor neurons in the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Rabies death from respiratory muscle paralysis (bulbar palsy)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Rabies is a:
questions.explanation: Rabies is caused by the rabies virus (Lyssavirus, Rhabdoviridae family). It is transmitted through animal bites via retrograde axonal transport to the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Rabies is a viral infection (rabies virus, Rhabdoviridae)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Subarachnoid hemorrhage is due to:
questions.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage can result from trauma, rupture of congenital berry aneurysms, or vasculitis (inflammation of Circle of Willis vessels). All options are correct causes.
questions.keyConcept: SAH: trauma, berry aneurysm rupture, or vasculitis (all of the above)
options: Inflammation of the vessels of the circle of Willis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following antiepileptic drugs is not an enzyme inducer?
questions.explanation: Valproate is not a CYP enzyme inducer; it actually inhibits some cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are all enzyme inducers that increase metabolism of other drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate is NOT an enzyme inducer (unlike phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a wrong statement regarding antiepileptic drugs?
questions.explanation: Pregnant women with epilepsy should NOT discontinue antiepileptic drugs abruptly - the risk of seizures may outweigh the risks of the medication. Treatment should be continued with the lowest effective dose of the safest drug.
questions.keyConcept: Pregnant women should NOT discontinue AEDs abruptly (risky to mother and fetus) - FALSE
options: Females who get pregnant should discontinue the antiepileptic drug
They are contraindicated in neuropathic pain
Carbamazepine antagonizes the action of antidiuretic hormone

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anesthetic agents is not acting through increase GABA activity?
questions.explanation: Ketamine acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist, not through GABA enhancement. Halothane, propofol, and isoflurane all enhance GABA-A receptor activity (inhibitory neurotransmitter).
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine acts on NMDA receptors, not through GABA enhancement

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following opioid drug should be avoided in patient taking MAOI:
questions.explanation: Meperidine (pethidine) should be avoided with MAOIs due to risk of serotonin syndrome and severe adverse reactions. It has serotonergic properties unlike other opioids. Morphine, fentanyl, and codeine do not have this specific interaction.
questions.keyConcept: Meperidine contraindicated with MAOIs (serotonin syndrome risk)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following antiepileptic drug is not preferred in pregnancy:
questions.explanation: Valproate is teratogenic (neural tube defects) and should be avoided in pregnancy. Lamotrigine and carbamazepine are safer options but still require careful risk-benefit analysis. All AEDs have some risk.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate is most teratogenic AED, not preferred in pregnancy

questions.keyConcept: Meperidine's metabolite normeperidine accumulates in renal failure and can cause neurotoxicity including seizures.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not true about local anesthetics:
questions.explanation: Bupivacaine is a long-acting local anesthetic, not short-acting. Adding sodium bicarbonate speeds onset by increasing the proportion of base form. Lidocaine is indeed an amide-type LA. Benzocaine is used topically.
questions.keyConcept: Bupivacaine is a long-acting local anesthetic, distinguishing it from short-acting agents like lidocaine.
options: Adding sodium bicarbonate increases activity of local anesthetics
Benzocaine is used as surface anesthetic

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following antiepileptic drug is not an enzyme inducer:
questions.explanation: Valproate inhibits hepatic enzymes and is actually an enzyme inhibitor, not an inducer. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital are all enzyme inducers that increase metabolism of many drugs.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate is unique among antiepileptics as an enzyme inhibitor rather than an enzyme inducer.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following anesthetic agent is not acting through increase GABA activity:
questions.explanation: Ketamine acts primarily as an NMDA receptor antagonist, producing dissociative anesthesia. Halothane, propofol, and isoflurane all potentiate GABA-A receptor activity to produce anesthesia.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine is unique among anesthetics in primarily acting on NMDA receptors rather than GABA.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Parkinson’s disease is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease features lead-pipe rigidity (uniform increase in tone throughout range), resting tremor (improves with movement), bradykinesia, and postural instability. Cogwheel rigidity is also seen with tremor.
questions.keyConcept: Lead-pipe rigidity is a cardinal feature of Parkinsonism, reflecting uniform increased muscle tone.
options: Paralysis of one side of the body.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the crucial event in the pathogenesis of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)?
questions.explanation: The crucial event in AD pathogenesis is abnormal amyloid-beta (A-beta) accumulation from proteolytic cleavage of APP by beta and gamma secretases, forming extracellular plaques that trigger neurofibrillary tangle formation and neuronal death.
questions.keyConcept: Amyloid-beta plaque deposition is the initiating pathological event in Alzheimer's disease.
options: Accumulation of Beta Amyloid Peptide (AB) in the brain over time

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the role of Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) in Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)?
questions.explanation: In AD, APP is abnormally cleaved by beta and gamma secretases (not alpha secretase) producing amyloid-beta 40/42 fragments that aggregate into toxic plaques. Mutations in APP gene cause familial AD.
questions.keyConcept: APP processing by abnormal secretase pathways produces neurotoxic amyloid-beta in Alzheimer's disease.
options: APP is sequentially cleaved by enzymes to generate AB.
APP is involved in the formation of neurofibrillary tangles.
APP is responsible for the degradation of beta amyloid peptide.
APP is a receptor for beta amyloid peptide.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is the major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s Disease?
questions.explanation: The epsilon 4 allele of apolipoprotein E (APOE4) is the major genetic risk factor for late-onset familial and sporadic AD, increasing risk 3-15 fold compared to epsilon 3.
questions.keyConcept: APOE4 is the strongest genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, influencing amyloid clearance and inflammation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s Disease?
questions.explanation: Model Answer: APOE4 (Apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 allele) is the major genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's Disease. Individuals carrying one copy have 3-4x increased risk, while homozygous carriers have 10-15x increased risk. APOE4 impairs amyloid clearance and promotes amyloid fibril formation.
questions.keyConcept: APOE4 polymorphism is the primary genetic determinant of AD risk through effects on amyloid metabolism.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What gene mutations cause autosomal dominant Parkinson's Disease?
questions.explanation: Model Answer: Autosomal dominant Parkinson's Disease is primarily caused by mutations in: 1) SNCA gene (alpha-synuclein) on chromosome 4 - causes protein aggregation, 2) LRRK2 gene (leucine-rich repeat kinase 2) - most common cause of familial PD, 3) Parkin (PARK2), PINK1, and DJ-1 genes - associated with mitochondrial dysfunction.
questions.keyConcept: PD-causing genes affect protein aggregation (SNCA), kinase activity (LRRK2), or mitochondrial function (Parkin, PINK1).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 55-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking and swallowing. On examination, he has atrophy and deviation of the tongue to the right side. He also shows loss of vibration and proprioception on the left side of his body and loss of pain and temperature on the left side of his body. Most likely site of lesion:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve (CN X) provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart, lungs, and GI tract. Damage causes dysphagia (swallowing difficulty) and dysphonia (voice changes) due to loss of laryngeal innervation.
questions.keyConcept: CN X parasympathetic fibers control GI motility and cardiac rhythm; damage causes dysphagia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The pain analgesic system includes which structure?
questions.explanation: The periaqueductal gray matter in the midbrain is a key component of the descending pain inhibitory system, connecting to nucleus raphe magnus and inhibiting dorsal horn pain transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Periaqueductal gray is the central controller of descending pain inhibition to dorsal horn.
options: Local cord neurons which secrete serotonin
Local cord neurons which secrete endorphin

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which is correctly matched regarding the pain analgesic system?
questions.explanation: The periaqueductal gray matter is the origin of descending pain inhibitory pathways that project to nucleus raphe magnus and release opioids to inhibit dorsal horn pain transmission.
questions.keyConcept: PAG is the key origin of descending analgesic pathways utilizing endogenous opioids.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which opioid is a long‑acting, pure agonist associated with milder withdrawal symptoms?
questions.explanation: Methadone is a long-acting pure mu-opioid agonist used in opioid maintenance therapy, producing milder withdrawal due to its slow dissociation from receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Methadone pharmacology

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which opioid acts as a partial agonist at the μ receptor and is used in opioid dependence management?
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist and kappa antagonist, producing ceiling effects on respiratory depression and milder withdrawal.
questions.keyConcept: Buprenorphine mechanism

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An alcoholic patient shows dependence related to activation of opioid receptors. Which drug is used for treatment?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone is a long-acting opioid antagonist used to prevent relapse in alcohol dependence by blocking opioid receptors involved in reward pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Naltrexone for alcoholism

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which anti‑Parkinsonian drug commonly produces atropine‑like adverse effects (dry mouth, blurred vision)?
questions.explanation: Benztropine is an anticholinergic anti-Parkinsonian drug that produces peripheral atropine-like side effects including dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention.
questions.keyConcept: Anticholinergic Parkinson drugs

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is used as a rescue therapy to manage sudden episodes of motor deterioration in Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is a rapid-acting dopamine agonist used subcutaneously as rescue therapy for sudden off episodes (akinesia) in advanced Parkinson's disease.
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine rescue therapy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which drug is used for tremors (in Parkinson’s)?
questions.explanation: Benztropine (anticholinergic) is particularly effective for tremor in Parkinson's disease, acting by blocking excessive cholinergic activity in the striatum.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonian tremor treatment

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Poliomyelitis is a:
questions.explanation: Poliomyelitis is caused by poliovirus (enterovirus), a single-stranded RNA virus that selectively targets motor neurons in the anterior horn.
questions.keyConcept: Poliomyelitis etiology

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Poliomyelitis is usually an infection of:
questions.explanation: Poliovirus specifically infects and destroys anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) of the spinal cord, causing flaccid paralysis.
questions.keyConcept: Polio pathogenesis
options: Anterior horn cells of the spinal cord
Posterior horn cells of the spinal cord

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Mode of infection in poliomyelitis is:
questions.explanation: Poliomyelitis spreads via the fecal-oral route, primarily through ingestion of contaminated food or water, with feces being the main source of viral shedding.
questions.keyConcept: Polio transmission
options: Ingestion of contaminated food or drink
Blood spread from a septic focus

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Muscle paralysis in case of poliomyelitis is due to:
questions.explanation: Poliovirus directly destroys anterior horn motor neurons, leading to denervation of skeletal muscles and subsequent flaccid paralysis without sensory loss.
questions.keyConcept: Polio paralysis mechanism
questions.modelAnswer: Poliomyelitis is caused by poliovirus which selectively targets and destroys the anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) of the spinal cord. The destruction of these motor neurons leads to denervation of the corresponding skeletal muscles, resulting in flaccid paralysis. Since the sensory neurons in the posterior horn are spared, there is no sensory loss associated with this paralysis. The extent of paralysis depends on the number and location of motor neurons destroyed.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient shows definite weakness of the right facial muscles while facial skin sensation is normal. On testing of the ocular movements, there is evidence of slight weakness of the right lateral rectus muscle. Radiology reveals the presence of tumour. Locate the possible site of the tumour.
questions.explanation: Inferior pons lesion affecting CN VI nucleus causes facial weakness (CN VII) and lateral rectus weakness (CN VI), with normal sensation pointing to a pontine tumor.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior pons lesion
options: Closed medulla at level of motor decussation.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 28‑year‑old woman has unilateral tinnitus, vertigo, and progressive hearing loss. MRI reveals a 3 cm mass at the cerebellopontine angle. Which microscopic finding is most characteristic?
questions.explanation: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) at cerebellopontine angle shows Antoni A (cellular) and Antoni B (hypocellular) areas with verocay bodies.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular schwannoma
options: Whorled spindle cells with psammoma bodies
Hypo‑ and hypercellular areas (Antoni A and B)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 5‑year‑old boy has recent‑onset gait instability and ataxia. MRI shows a midline posterior fossa mass. Biopsy reveals sheets of primitive small round cells with many mitoses. Which cytogenetic abnormality is most common?
questions.explanation: Medulloblastoma shows loss of chromosome 17p; it's a small round blue cell tumor of the posterior fossa in children.
questions.keyConcept: Medulloblastoma genetics
options: Loss of the short arm of chromosome 17 (17p)
Loss of the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which antiepileptic drug is associated with the highest risk of neonatal cleft lip and cleft palate?
questions.explanation: Phenytoin is associated with fetal hydantoin syndrome causing cleft lip/palate, digital hypoplasia, and growth retardation.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin teratogenicity

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which drug is used as a rescue medication for sudden akinetic episodes (off‑periods) in advanced Parkinson’s disease?
questions.explanation: Apomorphine (subcutaneous dopamine agonist) is used as rescue therapy for sudden off-periods in advanced Parkinson's disease.
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine for off-periods

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Antipsychotic‑induced akathisia is best treated with:
questions.explanation: Propranolol (beta-blocker) is first-line treatment for antipsychotic-induced akathisia, likely by blocking beta-2 receptors in the locus coeruleus.
questions.keyConcept: Akathisia treatment

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which antiepileptic is used as migraine prophylaxis and can cause weight loss and renal stones?
questions.explanation: Topiramate is used for migraine prophylaxis and causes weight loss and renal calcium phosphate stones (carbonic anhydrase inhibition).
questions.keyConcept: Topiramate uses

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which antidepressant is approved for management of chronic neuropathic pain (e.g., diabetic neuropathy)?
questions.explanation: Venlafaxine (SNRI) and duloxetine are antidepressants approved for diabetic neuropathy and other chronic pain conditions.
questions.keyConcept: Antidepressants for neuropathic pain

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which statement about ester local anesthetics is false?
questions.explanation: Ester local anesthetics are MORE liable to cause allergic reactions due to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite, not less.
questions.keyConcept: Ester local anesthetic allergy
options: They are hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterases.
Procaine is a member of this group.
They are shorter acting than amides.
They are less liable to induce allergy.
They are less liable to systemic toxicity than amides.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which opioid antagonist is also used to reduce alcohol craving?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone (opioid antagonist) is used in alcohol dependence treatment by blocking opioid receptors involved in the rewarding effects of alcohol.
questions.keyConcept: Naltrexone alcohol use

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which antiviral drug is used to treat neonates with herpes simplex virus encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Acyclovir (guanine analog) is the treatment of choice for HSV encephalitis in neonates, reducing mortality when given early.
questions.keyConcept: HSV encephalitis treatment

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: In a suspected case of rabies, the most important specimen for virus detection is:
questions.explanation: Saliva contains the highest concentration of rabies virus; a skin biopsy from the nape of the neck (hair follicles) is also used for fluorescent antibody testing.
questions.keyConcept: Rabies diagnosis specimen

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which is a cannabinoid drug used for management of hashish (cannabis) dependence?
questions.explanation: Dronabinol (synthetic THC) is used medically for cannabis dependence, providing agonist effects that reduce withdrawal and craving.
questions.keyConcept: Cannabinoid dependence treatment

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Pontine hemorrhage causes:
questions.explanation: Pontine hemorrhage typically damages bilateral corticospinal and autonomic pathways, causing pinpoint pupils (loss of pupillary light reflex), hyperpyrexia (autonomic dysregulation), and quadriplegia.
questions.keyConcept: Pontine hemorrhage: pinpoint pupils, hyperpyrexia, quadriplegia.
questions.modelAnswer: Pinpoint pupil, hyperpyrexia, quadriplegia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Extradural vs Subdural hemorrhage:
questions.explanation: Extradural hemorrhage results from middle meningeal artery rupture causing arterial bleeding with rapid accumulation and lucid interval, while subdural hemorrhage involves bridging veins causing slower venous accumulation.
questions.keyConcept: Extradural: arterial (meningeal); Subdural: venous (bridging veins).
questions.modelAnswer: Extradural: arterial (middle meningeal); Subdural: venous.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Excitation of the RAS occurs by:
A. Signals from the sleep centers
B. Analeptic drugs
C. Anesthetics
D. Lack of cortical signals
E. Vascular lesion
questions.explanation: Analeptic drugs (like doxapram) stimulate the reticular activating system by exciting respiratory and vasomotor centers, making them useful in CNS depression.
questions.keyConcept: Analeptic drugs excite the RAS.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Hemorrhage reaching the ……… layer of the scalp can cause black eye.
questions.explanation: Blood in the loose areolar tissue layer (subaponeurotic space) of the scalp can track around the orbit producing 'black eye' (periorbital ecchymosis).
questions.keyConcept: Black eye: hemorrhage in loose connective tissue layer of scalp.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is true about the intracranial hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Subdural hemorrhage crosses suture lines because it's venous bleeding with low pressure that accumulates slowly, unlike arterial extradural bleeding which is confined by suture attachments.
questions.keyConcept: Subdural bleeding crosses suture lines (venous).
options: Extradural bleeding means bleeding between dura and arachnoid maters.
Extradural bleeding is commonly venous in origin.
Subdural bleeding is commonly arterial in origin.
Subdural bleeding crosses the suture line.
